claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 exhibits a hierarchical heterostructure containing nanoscale phase interfaces and reticulated microstructural features.
The nanoscale interfaces and reticulated features mediate local stress distribution in HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed model will learn interface density and phase-boundary descriptors from high-resolution imaging and simulation data.
The learned descriptors will be incorporated into a reduced-order multiscale simulation framework.
The hierarchical structure of HfNbTiVAl10 remains stable during room-temperature, quasi-static testing at moderate strain rates.
Nanoscale phase interfaces and hierarchical heterogeneities govern local stress redistribution in HfNbTiVAl10.
Nanoscale phase interfaces and hierarchical heterogeneities govern the initiation of plastic deformation and fracture.
Microstructural descriptors can translate the effects of local heterogeneities into macroscopic mechanical responses.
A reduced-order surrogate can bypass extensive atomistic resolution while maintaining predictive accuracy.
The framework will predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness within ±15% of experimental measurements.
The framework will reduce total simulation runtime by approximately 30% relative to full-scale molecular dynamics or DFT simulations.
Established full-scale molecular-dynamics or first-principles methods require exhaustive atomistic resolution and longer computation times.
Established simulations typically have higher predictive uncertainty in heterogeneous alloy systems.
Dynamic microstructural evolution at high strain rates or extreme temperatures may invalidate fixed microstructural descriptors and cause the framework to fail.
Unexpected secondary-phase transformations may cause deviations from predictions based on the assumed descriptors.
Predictive performance may vary with microstructural variability, imaging-data quality, and the extent to which hierarchical features control deformation.
Independent tensile and fracture measurements, together with a runtime comparison against established atomistic simulations, can test the proposed framework.
The hypothesis is declared falsified if prediction errors exceed ±15% and the runtime reduction is less than 30%.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis promises both ±15% accuracy and a 30% runtime reduction, but the falsification rule requires both targets to fail simultaneously. Failure of either promised target alone would violate the hypothesis yet would not trigger the stated rule.
